segments.speaker: Dr. Nguyen
segments.text: I'm Dr. Nguyen. In the next ninety seconds, we'll calibrate our intuition for Gibbs free energy.

segments.speaker: Dr. Nguyen
segments.text: Delta G equals delta H minus temperature times delta S. It compares the energy available before and after a change.

segments.speaker: Dr. Nguyen
segments.text: When delta G is negative, the change is thermodynamically spontaneous under those conditions.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Does spontaneous mean the reaction happens fast, like the moment we mix the chemicals?

segments.speaker: Dr. Nguyen
segments.text: Good question. Spontaneous is willing, not necessarily speedy.

segments.speaker: Dr. Nguyen
segments.text: A diamond is willing to become graphite, but it takes its time about it.

segments.visual: A reaction-progress diagram rises to an activation-energy crest and settles lower. A vertical arrow labels the energy difference as negative delta G.

segments.speaker: Dr. Nguyen
segments.text: Negative delta G favors products. At zero, the system is at equilibrium. Positive delta G favors reactants.

segments.speaker: Dr. Nguyen
segments.text: So the sign tells us the favored direction, not the clock speed.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Direction, not speed. That distinction is the useful part.

segments.speaker: Dr. Nguyen
segments.text: Exactly. I'm Dr. Nguyen, and that's your Gibbs free energy calibration.
